definition.text: The amount of an ecosystem's growth that can be harvested while still letting it recover.

facts.text: It is most often measured in forestry, where sustainable forestry harvests no more wood in a year than grew that year in a given patch.
If more is consumed than is renewed, the ecosystem's carrying capacity shrinks over time.
It is a theoretical quantity that can only be estimated, and it depends on the recovery period chosen: three years' sustainable harvest is not necessarily three times one year's.
Firms that borrow to buy land rights may face debt that demands more yield than the land can renew, and the winner's curse leads winning bidders to overestimate it.
Only about 10% of biomass passes from prey to predator, so 100 kg of plants may yield 10 kg of herbivores and 1 kg of carnivores.
In 1986 Vitousek and colleagues estimated humans use 50 billion tons of photosynthetic biomass a year, 20% to 40% of the Earth's photosynthesis.
Measuring ecological footprints accurately requires estimating land productivity, that is, ecological yield.

definition.text: A bell-shaped curve approximating how a resource's production rate rises, peaks and falls over time.

facts.text: Geologist M. King Hubbert first presented it in 1956 to the American Petroleum Institute.
Using the 1948 peak in oil well discoveries, Hubbert predicted that oil production in the contiguous United States would peak around 1970.
It is a symmetric logistic distribution curve, often confused with the normal (Gaussian) curve, which it resembles.
Real production curves are often lopsided because of new extraction techniques, competing resources and government regulation.
US output followed the curve for 35 years after the early-1970s peak, but new extraction methods pushed it to a record 10.07 million barrels a day in November 2017.
It has been applied to natural gas, coal, uranium, copper, helium and water, and a modified version fits any resource harvested faster than it is replaced.

definition.text: The principle that the rent of a piece of land equals the extra output it produces compared with the best land available rent-free, using the same labour and capital.

facts.text: David Ricardo formulated it around 1809 and set it out fully in On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation; it is the origin of the term Ricardian rent.
In Ricardo's example, plots yield 100, 90 and 80 units of corn; once the 90-unit plot must be farmed, the best plot earns a rent of 10 units.
Ricardo argued that 'corn is not high because a rent is paid, but rent is paid because corn is high'.
The output of the best rent-free land is called the margin of production; rent is the difference between a site's productive capacity and this margin.
It applies to urban and rural land alike, and to any natural factor of production that is privately owned.
Ricardian rent differs from contract rent, the actual payments tenants make for using others' property.
